title: 100% olive oil Castile soap
subtitle: The traditional mild soap of the Mediterranean
excerpt: A cold-process bar made from 100% olive oil, the traditional Castile formula. Produces a mild, conditioning bar with a creamy rather than bubbly lather. Longer cure than blended soaps: 6 to 12 months for full hardness. Makes 7 bars.
sourceNotes: Castile soap origin documented in Anne Bramson, Soap: Making It, Enjoying It (1972). Olive oil SAP value 0.134 (NaOH per gram of oil, confirmed against SoapCalc and Bramble Berry SAP table v2023). 5% superfat applied. Water as 33% of oil weight. Olive oil fatty acid profile: USDA AOCS database (oleic, palmitic, linoleic).

recipe.batchNotes: Run any weight change through a lye calculator before making. Castile scales well to 1 kg; keep the water-to-oil percentage the same.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Full cure is 6 to 12 months: a longer cure produces a harder, milder bar. The bar is usable from 4 weeks but improves substantially over 6 months.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: Stores three years or more in a cool dark cupboard once fully cured. A well-cured Castile bar is very resistant to DOS (dreaded orange spots). Discard if the bar develops orange oily patches or smells sharp and paint-like.

glossaryTerms.definition: A bar soap made entirely or predominantly from olive oil, named after the Castile region of Spain. Pure Castile produces a mild, conditioning lather low in bubbly foam. It hardens slowly and becomes long-lasting given a full 6 to 12 month maturation.
The chemical reaction between fat and sodium hydroxide (lye) that produces soap and glycerine. Each oil has a SAP value: the grams of lye needed to fully saponify one gram of that oil.

The percentage of fat left unsaponified in the finished bar, typically 5 to 8%. At 5% superfat in Castile, the bar retains a small reserve of free olive oil that makes it conditioning without being greasy.
The point at which soap batter thickens enough that a drizzle on the surface briefly holds its shape. The signal that oils and lye have emulsified and the batter is ready to pour.

projectSchedule.title: Unmould and cut
projectSchedule.body: Turn out the loaf. Castile is very soft at this stage; if the bar feels sticky or gel-like, leave it another 24 to 48 hours in the mould before cutting. Wear protective gloves: the bar is still caustic.

projectSchedule.title: Four-week check
projectSchedule.body: The bars should be noticeably firmer. The lather will be present but small-bubbled and creamy. The soap is safe to use from this point, though not yet at full hardness.

projectSchedule.title: Six-month milestone
projectSchedule.body: A 6-month Castile bar is firm, pale gold, and noticeably milder than it was at four weeks. The lather is creamy and long-lasting. This is the earliest point at which a Castile bar is worth gifting.

projectSchedule.title: One-year cure
projectSchedule.body: A fully year-cured Castile bar is exceptional: very hard, very mild, very long-lasting. Store wrapped in paper in a cool dark cupboard.

content.text: is a 100% olive oil cold-process bar: mild, conditioning, and slow to cure. This formula uses 500 g olive oil at 5%

of olive oil produces a bar high in oleic acid: soft on skin and long-lasting in the cupboard. Cure time is the main constraint: six months for a good bar, twelve for an exceptional one. The lather is creamy and conditioning rather than bubbly and quick.
Put on protective gloves and goggles before handling lye. Read the full lye-handling method before starting.

items.prepNote: 100% of oil weight; extra-light or pure olive oil preferred for a paler bar
NaOH at 99% purity; calculated for 5% superfat on pure olive oil (SAP 0.134)

content.text: Work in a ventilated space wearing protective gloves and goggles. Pour the distilled water into the HDPE lye pitcher. Weigh the sodium hydroxide into a separate dry container. Add the lye to the water in a steady stream while stirring. Never add water to lye. The solution heats sharply to around 90°C and releases fumes; stand back. Set aside to cool to 38 to 42°C.

Weigh the olive oil into a stainless-steel or heatproof bowl. Olive oil is liquid at room temperature, so no melting is needed. If the oil is cold from storage, bring to room temperature. The oil should be between 35 and 45°C when the lye solution is added.

When both the lye solution and the oils are within a few degrees of each other (38 to 42°C), pour the lye solution into the oils in a thin stream, stirring as you go. Use the stick blender in short bursts of 10 to 15 seconds, alternating with hand-stirring. Castile reaches
more slowly than blended oils; allow 10 to 20 minutes of stick-blending for a light trace. The batter should have the consistency of thin custard before you pour.

Pour the batter into the silicone loaf mould. Smooth the top with a spatula. Wrap the mould in a towel to insulate it. Leave undisturbed for 24 to 48 hours. Castile soap gel phase is normal and produces a translucent amber centre zone on cutting; it fades as the bar matures over the following weeks.

Castile bars remain soft for longer than blended bars. After two days, check the soap: if it is still gel-like or sticky, leave it another 48 hours. Once the loaf can be handled without sticking, turn it out and cut into bars wearing protective gloves. Arrange on a rack with space between bars. Cure in a cool, dry space out of direct sunlight.

At four weeks the bar is safe to use but still fairly soft and the lather is minimal. At 12 weeks the bar is noticeably firmer with a gentle, creamy lather. At six months it is excellent. At twelve months it is the Castile bar that soapers give as gifts. Turn the bars every two weeks during the cure.

Store cured bars on an open rack in a cool, dark cupboard. Three years or more for a well-cured bar. Castile is resistant to DOS (dreaded orange spots, rancid superfat) because olive oil is high in stable oleic acid. Discard only if orange patches or a sharp paint-like smell appear.
